title: F against M
text:
SHERIFFDOM OF SOUTH STRATHCLYDE, DUMFRIES AND GALLOWAY 
AT HAMILTON 
 
[2026] SC HAM 58 
HAM-F598-24 
JUDGMENT OF SHERIFF J SPEIR 
 
in the cause 
 
F 
 
Pursuer 
 
against 
 
M 
 
Defender 
 
Pursuer: JC Hughes, Solicitors 
Defender: Lorna MacLeod Family Law, Solicitors 
 
 
Hamilton 21 April 2026 
Interlocutor 
The Sheriff, having resumed consideration of the cause: 
1. Recalls all previous interim orders; 
2. Sustains the first plea in law for the pursuer and makes an order for contact between 
him and the child C for 6 hours every fortnight on a Saturday between the hours of 10.00am 
and 4.00pm, or on such other day and for such other times as the parties may agree, and 
subject to the condition that the pursuer does not consume alcohol before or during contact; 
3. Makes a specific issue order allowing the defender to take C furth of the United 
Kingdom for the purpose of foreign travel and holidays for up to two weeks at a time so

2 
long as within C’s school holiday periods or otherwise with the consent of the pursuer 
failing which by court order; and 
4. Finds no expenses due to or by either party. 
 
Findings in Fact: 
1. The pursuer and defender are the father (F) and mother (M), respectively of the child 
(C) born in 2018. 
2. The parties were in a relationship from 2015 until their separation in September 2022. 
3. C has been diagnosed as being on the Autistic Disorder Spectrum and would be 
classed as highly autistic and pre-verbal. He requires significant additional support and 
routine. He attends an additional needs school. He is unable to express a view on the issue 
of contact with the pursuer. 
4. The defender has been the primary carer of C since birth. Prior to the parties 
separation the pursuer was also involved in his day-to-day childcare for short periods which 
allowed the defender to undertake employment. 
5. C has resided solely with the defender following upon the parties separation. 
6. On separation the defender and her family tried to assist the defender in finding 
settled and suitable accommodation but his lifestyle and living arrangements remained 
chaotic because of his alcohol consumption. 
7. Since the parties separation all contact between C and the pursuer has been 
supervised and for short periods. 
8. Initially that contact took place weekly and was supervised by the defender. 
9. On occasion the pursuer would attend for said contact smelling of alcohol or 
apparently intoxicated.

3 
10. In or about June 2024 the defender terminated this contact arrangement due to the 
pursuer’s attendance being irregular and unreliable. 
11. In November 2024 the pursuer raised the current action seeking an order for contact. 
12. Since March 2025 supervised contact between the pursuer and C has taken place 
within a contact centre. That contact has taken place consistently and has been positive for 
C. 
13. The pursuer was able to care for C appropriately and safely during said supervised 
contact. 
14. There exists a loving and caring relationship between the pursuer and C. 
15. The pursuer has a long standing and ongoing problem with alcohol which he 
consumes to chronic excess. 
16. The results of two toxicology tests on the pursuer undertaken in March and 
May 2025 were suggestive of chronic excessive alcohol use on the part of the pursuer for the 
period between 26 November 2024 to 9 May 2025. 
17. The pursuer failed to comply without reasonable excuse with a court order dated 
5 November 2025 in terms of which he was ordained to undertake further toxicology testing 
for alcohol in advance of the proof. 
18. Despite his issues with alcohol the pursuer holds down a demanding job as a chef in 
which he is required to work between 60 and 70 hours per week. 
19. The pursuer has recently undergone certificated training in Understanding Autism at 
West College Scotland and is prepared and willing to undertake further training and 
instruction as required. 
20. The pursuer demonstrates insight into C’s condition and needs which is likely to be 
improved and enhanced by more extensive contact with him.

4 
21. Contact with the pursuer is in the best interests of C. 
22. Said contact should be regular and unsupervised but non-residential at the present 
time. 
 
Findings in Fact and Law: 
1. It is in the best interest of C that a contact order be made in favour of the pursuer to 
provide for non-residential contact with C on a regular basis. 
2. It is in the best interests of C that a specific issue order be made allowing the 
defender to take C furth of the United Kingdom for the purpose of foreign travel and 
holidays for up to 2 weeks at a time so long as within C’s school holiday periods. 
3. It is better for C that said orders are made than none at all. 
 
Note 
Introduction 
[1] This action is concerned with the nature and extent of what contact the pursuer 
should have with his son “C”. C resides with his mother, the defender. She has been the 
primary carer of him since birth and continues in that role following upon the parties’ 
separation in 2022. The defender is not opposed in principle to the pursuer having contact 
but does not consider that at present it is in his best interests for that contact to take place on 
a residential basis. To date all contact that the pursuer has had with C since the parties 
separation has been on a supervised basis. The pursuer seeks an order for contact without 
that restriction and for overnight contact on a residential basis. This then was the focus of 
the proof and the parties’ submissions.

5 
[2] At the proof the pursuer was represented by Mr Connolly and the defender by 
Ms MacLeod. Evidence was led from both parties and the defender’s sister, “S”, in 
relatively short compass commensurate with the narrow issue in dispute. The significant 
facts are set out in my findings in fact. Having regard to C’s condition it was quite properly 
agreed that his views should be dispensed with. 
 
Evidence for the pursuer 
[3] The pursuer was content to give his evidence in chief by way of affidavit. He is 
employed full-time as a chef. He commenced a relationship with the defender in 2015 
or 2016. They began living together before the birth of C in September 2018. Although the 
pregnancy was unplanned, both were delighted. Their relationship functioned well initially, 
but over time arguments increased, often relating to household clutter. Both parties drank 
socially and played online games together. The pursuer denied any problematic drinking 
during the relationship. Following C’s birth he was fully involved in childcare, including 
feeding, bathing, and changing him. He took a month off work to support the defender 
during maternity leave. For a period he cared for C during the day to enable the defender to 
go out to work. That continued when they both worked at the same hotel, him on nights 
and the defender during the day. His caring role increased during the COVID-19 period 
when he was unemployed. He has a strong emotional bond with his son. After the 
relationship broke down in 2022 he continued to have contact with C once or twice a week 
for around an hour always with the defender present. He considered that the defender 
unfairly rejected his suggestions for activities such as swimming, which he believes C would 
enjoy. He acknowledged that C was highly autistic and pre-verbal with a cognitive age of 
18–24 months. To improve his understanding, he had completed a college course on autism

6 
in August 2025 and was now better equipped to respond to C’s needs, including recognising 
triggers and managing meltdowns. He believes C trusts him and communicates affection 
through hugs and play. He does not accept that he cannot be trusted to care for C without 
supervision. His home is now clean, well-furnished, and suitable for overnight stays. He 
wanted increased contact, including the possibility of overnight care. He could offer C 
meaningful support and engagement. He accepted that two toxicology tests showed high 
levels of drinking but maintained that he only drunk socially, held down full-time 
employment, and was willing to undergo further testing or stop drinking entirely to 
maintain a relationship with his son. 
[4] In cross-examination he confirmed that his current contact with C was in terms of a 
court order providing for supervised contact at a contact centre for one hour per fortnight. 
He accepted that since he had separated from the defender that he had never exercised 
unsupervised contact with C. He was aware that the reason the defender had not agreed to 
this was because of concerns over his drinking and his education as to C’s condition and 
needs. He confirmed the contents of the certificates of analysis from Cranford Laboratories 
dated 10 March and 20 May 2025 both of which disclosed that on testing he was significantly 
over the threshold for chronic excessive alcohol use for the periods covered by the tests. He 
knew that the court had ordered him to undergo further testing in advance of the proof but 
had not been able to get time off work preceding commencement of the proof to do that. He 
worked 60 to 70 hours in a 6 day week. He had a Sunday off but there were not testing time 
slots available then. He continued to drink alcohol. His last drink had been a few days 
previously when he had had 2 glasses of wine. He discounted the defender’s concerns as 
she used to drink excessively with him when they were still together. He confirmed that he 
has attended at C’s school at parents nights. Although C was progressing well he was doing

7 
so at a slower rate than he should be. If he was allowed residential contact with C over a 
weekend he was confident that his employers would accommodate his hours to fit in with 
that. He had not produced a letter or other evidence to vouch that as he did not think that 
necessary but it would not have been a problem to have done so. If he had such time with C 
he believed there were a multitude of things they could do together including going to the 
park, driving to Largs, going to Troon where his mother lives and taking him swimming. 
The last time C had seen his paternal grandmother was at Christmas 2023. He believed that 
C still recognised her from photographs he showed him. He disputed that C was as limited 
in the activities open to him as the defender suggested and believed that if he had more time 
with him it would help him develop more. He accepted that it would not be possible for C 
to go ice skating for another 10 years or so. He was aware that C goes swimming with the 
school twice a week but had never observed this. If he had more time with C he had 
identified sessions at a local swimming pool which would be suitable for him. He was 
hopeful that with the passage of time that he and the defender would be able to agree on 
activities that he could do with C. He accepted that he would need to gain her trust by 
demonstrating that he was now educated as to C’s needs and that he could be relied upon. 
He accepted that he had never looked after C overnight on his own but he did not see that as 
an issue or problem as C had stayed overnight with people other than the defender, namely 
his maternal aunt and maternal grandmother. He considered that C was well capable of 
adapting to changes in routine of this nature. For instance the defender had recently been 
taking him abroad to Denmark for the purpose of visiting her fiancée. While routine was 
important C was capable with dealing with change so long as it was only one thing at a time. 
He was aware that the defender was prepared to agree him having unsupervised contact 
with C for a period of 2 hours at a time. If there was to be this change then it would be

8 
better to move straight to unsupervised overnight contact rather that making a succession of 
changes each of which would require to be managed with C. He was confident that he had 
the skill set and techniques to deal with any adverse reaction by C to the change in his 
routine including the possibility of a “melt down”. He would have no issue in calling 
defender for assistance if the circumstances required it but could not think what those might 
be except perhaps if C had some kind of accident and hurt himself. He felt equipped now 
that he had completed the course in Understanding Autism at West College Scotland and for 
which he had been issued with a certificate on 11 August 2025. In re-examination he 
rehearsed having looked after C in the period he was unemployed while the defender went 
out to work. He referenced examples from when he had been looking after C and had to 
deal with him having melt downs. He spoke to what C was interested in and what he 
enjoyed. He accepted that there were further courses he could take including the “Early 
Bird” course but had not been able to do so yet because of the demands of his employment. 
But there was other material online which he had used to educate himself further. He had 
not recently had any discussion with the pursuer on C’s specific needs as she had cut off all 
contact with him that contrasted with shortly after separation when communication was 
better. She had not given him a reason for breaking off contact. He accepted that he had 
drunk a lot in the past even the recent past because he had led a free and single life. Even 
though he had reduced his alcohol consumption because the threshold for chronic excessive 
alcohol use was so low he expected that if tested now it would still show that. He was 
prepared to undertake to abstain from alcohol for any period of time that C was in his care. 
He did not consider that he was dependent whatsoever on alcohol. He had experienced no 
difficulties in the contact centre with C who responded well to his calming voice and 
physical touch. He accepted that it would be to C’s benefit if he and the defender would

9 
better communicate and indicated that he had wanted to carry on with mediation but that 
the defender did not. He hoped for improved communication in the future. He agreed that 
C should not be subject to too many changes. If there was to be a move out of the contact 
centre then the new arrangements should be something that will be in place for a few 
months. Contact should be on a residential basis as he was sure that he could get C to a 
level beyond where he is now and introducing him to new experiences. The fact that C had 
been able to travel to Denmark and also go on a cruise with the defender supported his view 
that C was capable and able to take on new experiences. He deserved to be part of C’s life. 
In response to some questions from the Court the pursuer advised: that his mother could 
not attend to give evidence because she had been unable to get time off work; that his 
mother had never asked the defender for contact to C in her own right and that she had not 
accompanied him to the contact centre; that he currently did not visit his mother in Troon as 
he did not have a driving licence and had never sat a driving test; that he had abstained 
from alcohol between June 2024 and January 2025; and that if contact was restricted to non-
residential contact then he would like a period of approximately 9 or 10 hours beginning 
at 10.00am 
 
Evidence for the defender 
[5] The defender adopted her affidavit as her evidence in chief subject to some 
elaboration and response to the pursuer’s evidence. She is in part-time employment as a 
commercial cleaner. Her income therefrom is supplemented by receipt of universal credit. 
She was in a relationship with the pursuer from 2015 until their separation in 
September 2022. She also confirmed C’s condition and that because he is unable to 
communicate verbally he cannot meaningfully express a view on contact arrangements. In

10 
the early years of the parties’ relationship both she and the pursuer were in employment but 
that because he lost his job during COVID -19 times she was the sole bread winner which 
meant that the pursuer was responsible for caring for C while she worked. She was 
concerned however that he appeared to have spent much of this time drinking and playing 
computer games rather than focusing on meeting C’s physical or emotional needs. 
Following the parties separation she and her parents and other family members assisted the 
pursuer in moving into a two-bedroom flat following a period he had spent in homeless 
accommodation. The flat was an unsuitable environment in which to care for C due to it 
being in a state of disorder and missing appropriate flooring and furnishings. It was also 
littered with empty alcohol bottles, cigarette butts and mouldy food. She had not visited it 
since 2023. She was aware the child welfare reporter did not appear to have any concerns on 
that front when she did a report in March 2025. C had never been to the flat. She had 
concerns as to how C would cope with a new environment. It often takes him some time to 
adapt and settle down and sometimes he just would not. She gave an example of C not 
accepting the room in which a TKD class she took him to was held albeit he was better the 
next time they went. He reacted particularly badly to noise and confined environments. If 
he had a meltdown he would scream, lie on the floor and kick out. She gave examples of 
this happening in a service station while on a trip to Blackpool and recently in Lidl store a 
few months previously. He no longer slept over at her parents’ house. He hadn’t slept over 
at her sister’s house since he was 4 or 5 years old. He has not had sleepovers with any 
friends. The advice she had received through the Early Bird support group was that most 
SEN children did not do sleepovers. Early Bird was an educational and support course she 
went on at the suggestion of her sister, S, whose child was also autistic. The defender 
continues to have concerns about the pursuer’s alcohol dependency and there have been

11 
multiple occasions where he arrived for contact smelling of alcohol or appeared intoxicated. 
Allied to these concerns were those related to C’s vulnerability. That is why she supervised 
contact in the period following separation. Usually this took place on Wednesdays after 
school for between 1 and 2 hours. She stopped contact in June 2024 because the pursuer 
became increasingly irregular and unreliable. He increasingly tried to change the 
arrangement at short notice. The pursuer was unrealistic as to the activities which C could 
safely undertake including swimming and ice-skating. C requires routine, stability, and 
familiar surroundings. C walks on his tip toes and was unable to walk long distances. He 
could quickly become tired and upset. She continues to believe that the pursuer does not 
understands those needs and the consequence of his communication being limited. She 
believed the pursuer still required further education as to how to deal with specific issues 
that arise for C but accepted that this would be most beneficial if it could be applied to 
actual practical situations. C does not have an ongoing relationship with the pursuer’s 
mother and on the last occasion he met her at Christmas 2023 he was distressed by her 
presence. She was firmly opposed to any extension of contact operating on a residential 
basis, until she could be satisfied as to the pursuer’s abstinence from alcohol and 
mindfulness as to C’s safety. When the defender first met the pursuer she also used to drink 
but stopped when she found out she was pregnant. After that she restricted alcohol 
consumption to special occasions. The pursuer’s alcohol consumption became worse after C 
was born. He would regularly drink between one and one and half litres of whisky in a 
24 hour period. She would often come home from work to find that him drinking and 
playing video games. He mostly drank whisky but occasionally also red wine or Buckfast. 
Further now that the pursuer was seeking residential contact every fortnight from Friday to 
Sunday rather than Saturday to Sunday (which is what he had craved in the initial writ)

12 
there was a further issue in relation to C being dropped off by the school bus on a Friday at 
around 3.00pm. The bus service will only drop off at the main carer’s address and nowhere 
else. There were some issues initially with C travelling by bus but now he was alright so 
long as he got a window seat. C enjoyed swimming and did this when organised through 
the school. She had not taken him swimming but he was capable of going in and out of the 
pool by himself. He might be prepared to go into the pool at the baths identified by the 
pursuer but it would depend on the atmosphere. She was unaware whether there were 
special sessions for children with disabilities. She did not consider that she was 
overprotective but rather that C had certain needs and was unable to do certain things that 
other children his age or younger could do. For that reason safeguards were required. She 
felt unable to trust the pursuer to recognise these limitations and safeguards. He required 
further education on them even if he could demonstrate abstinence from alcohol. She also 
did not trust him to call her if any issue arose during contact. Some aspects of his affidavit 
(particularly paragraph 10) caused her to doubt whether he had a true understanding of C’s 
condition. C was still undergoing assessment. There had been a recent improvement in C’s 
communication skills albeit numeracy remained an issue. He was still unable to articulate a 
sentence or express basic terms such as like/dislike or hot/cold but was able to say when he 
was happy and understand what that meant. She was unaware of the pursuer ever having 
abstained from alcohol and doubted that he could do so. She was not opposed in principle 
to contact between the pursuer and C so long as it was safe. C had no concept of danger. 
Any changes to routine had to be small and gradual. It would not be appropriate to increase 
the duration of non-residential contact to over 8 hours initially but it could get there over 
weeks or months. C did not have a concept of time but would act up if he did not like a

13 
particular environment, person or activity. He was most comfortable with familiarity and 
routine. 
[6] In cross-examination she readily accepted that C should have the pursuer in his life 
and to spend quality time with him so long as it was safe. She was prepared to work with 
the pursuer including re-attending mediation albeit she was sceptical as to the pursuer’s 
commitment. She agreed that the contact centre reports were positive and that C appeared 
comfortable with the pursuer in that environment. The pursuer’s excessive drinking had 
mostly been at the weekend but he drank every day. To date she had not been prepared to 
take his word or undertaking that he would stop drinking. She was engaged to be married. 
C had met her fiancé four times, once here and three times in Denmark for between 1 and 
2 weeks. They planned to spend Christmas together in Denmark and get married shortly 
afterwards with her fiancé relocating from Denmark to Scotland. She had not previously 
asked for the pursuer’s express permission to take C out of the country for these visits, as he 
knew they were taking place, but would now do so if required. C liked to fly so long as he 
had a window seat. On his first visit to Denmark he had been a bit restless but she was able 
to settle him after a few days once he accepted the new environment. 
[7] In response to questions from the court she suggested some activities that the 
pursuer could do with C during contact including going to soft play, an ice rink, having 
lunch and going to the cinema. During such times she would go home, go shopping or wait 
in her car in case she was required to assist. She remained resistant to the pursuer taking C 
to his home because of her concerns in relation to him drinking. Although the parties homes 
were close to one another, being just over a mile apart, this was too far for C to walk but it 
was a very short drive. Her current working hours were 9.30am-1.45pm Wednesday to 
Friday. She believed that C should have contact with his paternal grandmother. The

14 
defender was not on speaking terms with her because of things said in the past. She did not 
consider the explanation given by the pursuer for her not attending as a witness to be 
credible. 
[8] S is the sister of the defender. She adopted her affidavit as her evidence in chief with 
some brief elaboration. She had been the one to first identify that C was showing signs of 
autism when he was around one year old. She had particular insight because her own child 
was also autistic. She used to care more frequently for C when the defender was at work 
including overnight but that had reduced since the defender had changed jobs and C had 
started school. She was familiar with his daily routine including transport to and from 
school. She still looked after him overnight occasionally for instance during the last summer 
holidays. She does not believe that contact with the pursuer is in C’s best interests. She 
considers him an alcoholic and incapable of caring properly for C. In the past she has 
assisted in cleaning properties occupied by the pursuer and described them as unhygienic, 
unsafe and littered with rubbish and empty alcohol bottles, all of which were dangerous for 
C. She remembers a specific incident when the defender was too drunk to take C to nursery 
albeit he falsely claimed he was unwell. A subsequent visit by social work found alcohol 
within the child’s reach. She recalls that after this her sister stopped relying on the pursuer 
for childcare and she took over that role. She considered that overnight contact would be 
too drastic a change in C’s routine. She disagreed with the pursuer’s suggestion that one 
change would be better rather than a number of incremental changes. Routine was the most 
important thing along with finding activities that were enjoyed. In a very brief 
cross-examination she accepted that it was in C’s interests to see the pursuer but not 
overnight due to safety concerns.

15 
Submissions 
[9] I am grateful to both parties agents for their written submissions and draft proposed 
findings in fact. I do not propose to rehearse them at length suffice to say that the core 
propositions in each mirrored the position adopted by parties in evidence. Both parties 
were agreed that that the applicable law was to be found in section 11 of the Children 
(Scotland) Act 1995 
 
Pursuer 
[10] The pursuer seeks a contact order under section 11 of the Children (Scotland) 
Act 1995 in respect of C whose welfare is the court’s paramount consideration. Because C is 
non-verbal and has a diagnosis of autism with significant developmental delay, he cannot 
express his views directly. It is common ground that C has complex needs, including 
limited social skills, no safety awareness and unpredictable meltdowns. The pursuer 
understands these needs, has undertaken relevant coursework, and was actively involved in 
C’s care until the parties separated in 2022. After separation, contact became limited and 
supervised by the defender, leading to the present court action. Supervised contact at the 
contact centre has been positive, showing a strong bond between father and child. The 
defender’s main concern is the pursuer’s alcohol use: two tests demonstrated chronic use, 
and the pursuer failed to obtain a third test. His position however is that his drinking is not 
excessive but nonetheless is prepared to undertake not to drink during contact. The pursuer 
seeks unsupervised, alternating-weekend residential contact from Friday at 5.00pm until 
Sunday at 5.00pm. This was for longer than currently craved in his pleadings. Although 
this will be a change for C it has been shown that he can adapt to new routines, as shown by 
contact-centre sessions and trips abroad with the defender. Residential weekend contact

16 
will enable the father-child relationship to grow in a safe and structured way. Alternatively, 
in the event that the Court was not prepared to grant an order for residential contact then for 
non-residential contact for as long as was considered appropriate and in the best interests of 
C. 
 
Defender 
[11] The defender has been the primary carer of C since birth. Although the pursuer had 
more childcare responsibilities prior to the parties’ separation, which allowed the defender 
to work, it was often the case that he prioritised drinking and gaming over childcare and 
struggled to meet Cs needs. Initially after separation the contact which took place between 
the pursuer and C was short mid-week contact under her supervision. It involved quite 
limited activities due to C’s vulnerabilities. She remained concerned as to the pursuer’s 
ability to manage contact with C safely due to his alcohol dependency. Her concerns were 
supported by the toxicology reports from March and May 2025 showing chronic excessive 
intake. It was a matter of particular concern that the third test ordered by the court had not 
been undertaken. Although the pursuer now sought residential contact every fortnight he 
had not vouched the assertion that his employer, for whom he required to work up to 
70 hours per week would support this arrangement. Further she had no confidence that the 
defender could meet C’s substantial care needs or safely manage routine changes. The 
defender was not opposed to contact in principle but opposed residential or extended 
non-residential contact. She submitted that the existing fortnightly arrangement should 
continue outwith the contact centre but with a limited duration up to 3 hours. East Kilbride 
town centre would be a convenient meeting point as there were a number of activities close 
by that C would enjoy.

17 
 
Specific issue order 
[12] Separately the defender also seeks a specific issue order to allow her to take C out of 
the country to visit her fiancé in Denmark (though that would be short lived once he had 
moved to Scotland) and for holidays without having to obtain the pursuer’s express consent 
on each occasion. Although this issue was not addressed in the pleadings, nor was any 
evidence led in relation to it beyond the defender’s inadvertent omission to seek the 
pursuer’s consent to take C outwith the UK, the pursuer confirmed that he was not opposed 
to such an order being made so long as it was confined to school holiday periods. 
Accordingly it was agreed that I should make a specific issue order to reflect this agreed 
position. 
 
Decision and reasons 
[13] There were no significant issues of credibility and reliability which bore on the 
matters which required to be determined. Such issues as they were in main related to what 
are now fairly historic matters relating to the nature, extent and quality of the pursuer’s care 
of C prior to the parties separation. The significant exception to that generality relates to the 
pursuer’s alcohol consumption and how it bore on his ability to care for C. I discuss this 
further below. Where such issues arose I preferred the evidence of the defender as 
supported by S. Thereafter differences between the parties’ might be categorised more as 
matters of opinion and perception rather than of fact per se. 
[14] There was no issue that legal framework is contained in section 11 of the Children 
(Scotland) Act 1995. In short the court requires to prioritise the child’s welfare, consider 
whether making an order is better than making none, and—where possible—obtain the

18 
child’s views. Due to his needs, C was unable to express views to the Child Welfare 
Reporter, Mrs Fiona Carey. In any event, as I have noted, this is not a case in which there 
was any issue as to the principle of contact being in C’s best interests, rather what the nature 
and extent of that contact should be. 
[15] As I indicated at the conclusion of the hearing I was impressed by both parties’ 
obvious love and devotion towards their son. I was also impressed by the dignity and 
reserve shown by both parties during the course of the proceedings despite their differing 
views as to what arrangements were currently in C’s best interests. The crucial issue in this 
respect is whether an order for residential contact with the pursuer was in C’s best interests. 
I have little hesitation in determining that it is not at the present time. It is difficult to 
understand why the pursuer periled his application for such an order against a background 
where he has failed to obtemper the court order made on 5 November 2025 requiring him to 
undergo further toxicology testing for alcohol use or misuse. This order was made as part of 
the case management process. The need for the further test is patently obvious standing the 
results of the earlier tests carried out in March and May 2025 both of which disclosed 
chronic alcohol misuse. In this regard I note in passing that the pursuer’s assertion that he 
had abstained from alcohol between June 2024 and January 2025 bears to be contradicted by 
the terms of the first of those reports dated 10 March 2025 (no 6/3/1 of process). The findings 
in that report relate to the period approximately from 26 November 2024 to 24 February 
2025. 
[16] Accordingly I am entirely satisfied that the defender’s concern that alcohol 
consumption remains an issue for the pursuer is well founded. I do not accept the 
explanation proffered as to why he was unable to undergo a further test in advance of the 
proof. If his employers are prepared to be flexible to accommodate significant weekend

19 
contact with C, as he maintained, it beggars belief that they could not have afforded him a 
few hours off work to submit to a further toxicology test. While I consider that his 
undertaking not to consume alcohol while C was in his care an appropriate one, and have 
incorporated such abstinence into the order I have decided to make, I do not consider it 
sufficient to displace the valid concerns expressed by the defender as to the 
inappropriateness of allowing the pursuer to have residential contact with C until he can 
demonstrate a sustained period of sobriety or at the very least a moderate and safe level of 
alcohol consumption. 
[17] It is unfortunate that the pursuer elected to proceed to proof in the absence of such 
further testing, as there were clear indications that he had a greater degree of insight into C’s 
condition and needs that the defender was prepared to credit him with. I was impressed by 
his enthusiasm for wanting to apply the training he had obtained on the Understanding 
Autism course. I am prepared to accept at face value his willingness to undertake such 
further education and training as might be available. Accordingly I am satisfied that it is 
appropriate and in the best interests of C to make an order for non-residential contact to 
now take place every fortnight outwith the contact centre. Although the defender also 
recognised that this was an appropriate next step there remained an issue as to duration of 
such contact. The defender submitted that 3 hours was an appropriate starting point and if 
it went well it could be increased. The pursuer on the other hand proposed 9 hours. I 
consider that the appropriate duration is broadly in the middle, namely for 6 hours. This 
will allow the pursuer and C to undertake an activity, have a meal together and also enjoy 
some downtime. While the order I will make will prescribe the default position for this 
contact to take place on a Saturday between 10.00am and 4.00pm. I recognise that parties 
may wish to vary this by agreement to suit any other commitments or arrangements.

20 
Accordingly the order provides for such variation by mutual consent but in the absence of 
such consensus that it will be the default position. A similar consideration pertains to the 
location for drop off and collection of C. The defender suggested that could be East Kilbride 
Town Centre but I have not prescribed this in the order. Standing the proximity of the 
parties’ homes and the defender being able to drive then an alternative drop off and/or 
collection point could be the pursuer’s home. For the avoidance of doubt the order 
pronounced does not exclude the pursuer exercising all or part of the contact in his home. 
Previous concerns as to the appropriateness of that accommodation appear to have been 
removed by the investigations carried out and reported on by the Child Welfare Reporter. 
Indeed if the defender is able to see the property for herself then it may go somewhat to 
alleviating concerns she has expressed about its suitability for extended periods of contact, 
including potentially overnight in due course. 
[18] By corollary, now that contact is to move outside the contact centre and will be 
unsupervised, the pursuer might well find benefit in obtaining guidance and assistance in 
developing new techniques in managing C in situations where he is demonstrably 
uncomfortable. In this regard I would urge the pursuer to seek guidance from the defender 
as the person who has the best understanding of C’s needs and management techniques. I 
equally understand the pursuer’s wish to have his own independent space and time with C 
but I rather think that the chances of that developing successfully into a quality experience 
for both him and C would be increased if at least in the short term he was prepared to accept 
and use the valuable resource that the defender is. That of course would be dependent on 
the defender being prepared to assist and co-operate but I formed the clear impression that 
she wants contact between the pursuer and C to work and would be prepared to offer 
assistance and insight if asked to do so. In this regard I have had regard to the terms of

21 
section 11(7)(D) of the Children (Scotland) Act 1995 (the requirement for cooperation). 
While such cooperation is not a prerequisite for operation of the order I have made, I am 
cautiously optimistic from the parties previous engagement with one another both prior to 
litigation and thereafter their participation in inconclusive mediation, that this will take 
place when they both adjust their focus from these court proceedings to how C’s welfare 
and best interests might be met going forward. 
 
Expenses 
[19] Both parties were agreed that whatever the outcome I should make a finding of no 
expenses due to or by and accordingly that is what I shall do.
